Extending Interval Logic Tensor Networks (ILTN), tLTN grounds state predicates as fuzzy truth-value paths over time points, while events are first-class entities with learnable trapezoidal fuzzy durations and differentiable Allen-style relations. A compositional semantics fuses static, event-structural, and state-dynamic satisfaction into a single differentiable LTN grounding. Crucially, the modalities constrain each other bidirectionally: the interval layer dictates where point-wise constraints (e.g., Until, Since) are evaluated, restricting them to event-defined spans; conversely, the point-wise layer validates interval relations, rejecting them if underlying state dynamics contradict the relation. Through controlled synthetic examples, we show when single-modality learning fails and how this localization reduces frame-level computational cost on long traces.

title: Defending Vision-Language-Action Models against Transferable Attacks via Visual-Proprioceptive Consistency
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong capabilities in a wide range of robotic tasks. However, adversarial attacks in VLA models have shown strong transferability across robotic tasks, posing significant threats to robotic systems. Despite their different attack strategies, we observe that these transferable attacks share a common consequence: they disrupt the VLA model's perception towards the robot itself. Motivated by this observation, we propose a proprioception-grounded defense framework that leverages trusted proprioceptive information to detect and mitigate transferable adversarial attacks. Specifically, we utilize the robot's proprioceptive states to establish a trusted spatial reference, and compare it with the robot's perceived location inferred from visual features. Discrepancies between these two sources provide a reliable signal for detecting adversarial attacks. Extensive experiments demonstrate effective detection of transferable adversarial patches and improved closed-loop performance. Real-robot experiments further demonstrate the effectiveness of our defense on real-world robotic tasks.

title: ReSUL: Learning Regional Sensor Utility for Robust Multisensor Semantic Segmentation
summary: A corrupted sensor observation is not necessarily useless: misalignment can place informative scene structure at the wrong location. Robust multisensor segmentation must determine where to retain this evidence, where to exclude it, and where repair can recover its value. We introduce Regional Sensor Utility Learning (ReSUL), which learns these choices through their effect on segmentation risk. ReSUL compares full-sensor predictions, sensor-exclusion paths, and a re-registration path for displaced thermal inputs. A router predicts each path's signed reduction in category-balanced Brier risk relative to a fixed reference, then uses these estimates to allocate spatial mixture weights. This supervision connects spatial allocation to measurable task benefit without requiring fault labels at inference. MFNet experiments compare project-trained models under eleven clean and disturbed input conditions. ReSUL ranks first in 10 of 11 conditions in both ImageNet-1k and ImageNet-22k comparisons. Under severe thermal displacement, it reaches 54.58% and 55.63% mIoU, exceeding the strongest competing method in each group by 7.19 and 5.63 percentage points. Fixed-bank MFNet ablations show that utility supervision improves all eleven condition means over task-only routing. These results support learning how to use disturbed observations through their regional prediction benefit. Code is available at https://github.com/D-ST-Sword/ReSUL.

title: Rate-Quality-Energy Convex Hull for High Dynamic Range Adaptive Video Streaming
summary: High Dynamic Range (HDR) video introduces substantially higher decoding complexity and energy consumption than Standard Dynamic Range (SDR), yet most adaptive streaming pipelines still rely on bitrate ladders optimized using SDR-oriented metrics such as VMAF. These ladders fail to capture HDR-specific perceptual behavior and ignore decoder-side energy, resulting in energetically inefficient operating points. This work proposes a rate-quality-energy convex-hull optimization framework that jointly considers bitrate, HDR-aware perceptual quality (HDRVMAF), and client-side processing energy, including decoding and upscaling. Experiments on twelve 4K HDR sequences from the LIVE HDR Video Quality Assessment Database evaluate 72 representations per clip and demonstrate that traditional VMAF-optimized ladders frequently select high-resolution encodes that become dominated once energy is accounted for. Compared to the Default HLS ladder, our HDR-aware method achieves substantial bitrate savings of up to 54.34% at equal HDRVMAF, while yielding relative client-side energy reductions of up to 43.10% under higher energy weighting. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework as a practical foundation for constructing HDR bitrate ladders that explicitly expose and control perceptual quality-energy trade-offs.

title: Language models compress human preference geometry while political structure remains prompt-sensitive
comment: 13 pages, 6 figures, 34 pages of supplementary material
summary: Large language models are increasingly used to construct synthetic publics. Prior work has documented errors in individual responses, population heterogeneity, and prompt robustness, but whether these failures reflect a common loss of fidelity or distinct properties of synthetic populations remains unclear. We tested this using matched pairwise policy choices from 1,991 Chilean, 843 French, and 434 Brazilian adults replayed through three open-weight model families. Across a 27-condition Chilean grid and cross-country factorial replications, no condition jointly reproduced individual choices, population heterogeneity, and political organization. The most consistent result was compression of the latent preference space: synthetic participant variance was only 0.4-10.5% of the corresponding human reference in the primary comparisons and remained below human variance in all 270 matched refits. Political structure was much more sensitive to how choices were elicited. Reversing proposal position changed 12.3-31.2% of decoded choices. Explicitly labeling the endpoints of the numeric left-right self-placement scale changed 20.5-28.1% of choices and moved an independent proposal-level measure of left-right cleavage toward the human pattern in all three settings. Yet matched agreement improved by only 3.1-4.2 percentage points and participant geometry remained compressed. In Chile, the same intervention compressed the synthetic population further. These results separate political legibility from population fidelity: language models can recover salient political divisions while failing to preserve the breadth of human preference variation. Synthetic-public fidelity is therefore a property of the checkpoint, prompt, and setting, not of a checkpoint alone, and must be evaluated separately at individual, population, and political-structure levels.

title: Specialized Large Language Models for Markovian Reasoning: Structural Cache Compression, Transition Pretraining, and Dual-Loop Transformers
summary: Standard autoregressive large language models attend to the growing history of generated tokens, making the key-value (KV) cache a central memory and throughput bottleneck in long-chain reasoning and multi-branch sampling. Yet an important class of reasoning problems is naturally first-order Markovian: the next step depends on a sufficient representation of the current state, rather than on the raw sequence of all earlier steps. We develop a unified design paradigm for Markovian-reasoning specialized large language models. At the cache level, the Markovian state interface transforms history-dependent KV storage into constant-size state transfer with respect to the number of reasoning steps. At the learning level, we reformulate long-chain prediction as independently trainable one-step transition objectives, with explicit state bottlenecks, distillation, invariance, and drift-consistency losses. At the architectural level, we introduce a dual-loop Transformer: an outer loop advances the reasoning state, while an inner recurrent-depth loop allocates adaptive computation to each transition through shared weights and explicit memory tokens or recurrent matrix states. We connect this architecture to a three-region cache, step-relative positions, truncated backpropagation, branch-aware checkpoints, and a transition-centric evaluation protocol. The organizing principle is simple: the optimal reasoning system need not remember everything; it must carry forward exactly what the future needs. This principle opens a path toward specialized reasoning engines whose memory footprint is decoupled from reasoning-chain length.

title: Knowing What You Carry: Scalable Physics-Anchored World Models for Robotic Planning with Liquid Payloads
summary: Payload-carrying robots, such as delivery robots and autonomous trucks, must choose motions that keep them and their payload safe, so their planners predict the outcome of each candidate motion. Modern planners compare thousands of candidates per step on a GPU, using world models such as batched simulators or learned predictors. Most of them assume a rigid payload, but a liquid payload keeps moving after a maneuver, and its state is rarely measured. Near a safety limit, small prediction errors can make an unsafe plan look safe. Coupled fluid simulations are accurate but too costly for every candidate, while low-order slosh models are cheap but accurate only away from resonance. We study this trade-off on a ground vehicle with a partly filled tank near its rollover limit. First, we build PLiMB (Parallel Liquid-MultiBody), a GPU-parallel slosh simulator that, to our knowledge, couples FLIP liquid two-way with many multibody vehicles for the first time. It provides training data and a high-fidelity reference. Second, we propose a scalable physics-anchored world model that combines a modal-slosh and roll prior, an estimate of the hidden liquid state from the vehicle's own motion history (no sensor in the tank), and a learned correction. Without simulating the fluid, it scores thousands of candidate plans in one batched pass within a 20 Hz control tick on one GPU. We judge each world model by the plans it leads a planner to choose. Near the rollover limit, planners that treat the liquid as a rigid payload or use published low-order slosh models repeatedly pick unsafe plans when a safe one exists. Ours never does in our standard tank and makes about half as many in a wide tank whose sloshing mode lies in the maneuver band. There, the liquid state left by earlier driving can change the best plan, and reading it from the vehicle's history halves our model's near-limit prediction error.

title: UbiEnlight: User-Perception-Aware Real-Time Low-Light Video Enhancement on Mobile Devices and Smartglasses
summary: Low-light video capture is now common on smartphones and wearables, yet dynamic illumination coupled with mobile/werable user motion causes noise, blur, and flicker that make videos hard to perceive and use, especially for users with night blindness and near-eye displays. Prior work enhances frames with post-hoc temporal constraints or optimizes videos directly; however,low-light and motion degradations are spatiotemporally coupled, so post-hoc consistency after per-frame restoration often leaves flicker and motion artifacts. We present UbiEnlight, the first diffusion-transformer-based on-device system for real-time, temporally stable low-light video enhancement. UbiEnlight builds on two insights: (1) illumination and structure separate more robustly in the frequency domain, enabling a spectrum-guided diffusion transformer that injects Fourier amplitude/phase priors to correct illumination while anchoring structure without optical flow; and (2) user perceptual tolerance varies by context, motivating a perception-aware controller that adapts sampling depth, attention reuse, and frame caching at runtime. We implement UbiEnlight on smartphones and smartglasses, and evaluate it against state-of-the-art baselines. UbiEnlight improves temporal stability by up to 54.76% under dynamic/extreme conditions while sustaining real-time on-device performance.

title: PAC Infinite-Time Safety Guarantees for Stochastic Systems with Unknown Probabilistic Distributions
summary: This paper studies infinite-time safety certification for discrete-time stochastic systems with continuous dynamics and unknown disturbance distributions that have full support on a known compact disturbance set. We develop a probably approximately correct (PAC) data-driven framework that uses only finitely many i.i.d. disturbance samples: with confidence at least $1-δ$, if the certification procedure accepts a candidate certificate defining a nonempty subset of a prescribed compact safe set, then the system, starting from any state in this subset, remains within the safe set for all future times with probability at least $1-ε$. Our approach builds on a fundamental characterization of infinite-time safety. We first prove that a robust invariant set exists within a compact safe set if and only if there exists an initial state from which the system remains in the safe set indefinitely with positive probability. This reduces infinite-time safety certification to two tractable subproblems: robust invariant-set computation and finite-horizon reach-avoid certification. We first compute a robust invariant set within the safe set, then use i.i.d. disturbance samples to certify, with PAC guarantees, a subset of initial states for which the probability of reaching this set within a finite horizon while remaining safe is at least a prescribed threshold. To our knowledge, this is the first PAC framework for infinite-time safety under unknown disturbance distributions. Finally, illustrative examples demonstrate the method using semi-definite programming.

title: Beyond the section plane: Robust 3D reconstruction of multiplex immunofluorescence exposes limitations of 2D spatial cell statistics
summary: Spatial analysis of the tumour microenvironment with multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF) typically relies on single thin tissue sections, which misrepresent the 3D tissue organisation and bias spatial cell statistics in ways that remain largely unquantified. We reconstruct 24 breast and lung tumour tissue microarray cores in 3D, each from 15-20 serial mIF sections, and compare spatial cell statistics in 3D with those from individual sections. Our pipeline combines affine pre-alignment with dense deformable refinement using RoMa v2, achieving a median target registration error of 1.79 $μ$m, well below nuclear size, which allows nuclei to be linked across sections. While cell-type proportions are preserved in 2D (Pearson corr. $r \geq 0.99$), 3D analysis reveals up to 3.8 times shorter nearest-neighbour distances, 13-19% higher neighbourhood entropy, and 2-4 times more contacts per cell. Tissue composition can thus be reliably estimated from individual sections, whereas cell-cell interactions require volumetric analysis.

title: Muted Distillation: Sealing Reasoning from Teacher Unlocks Token-Efficient Agents
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) is commonly adopted as one of the components in post-training of large language models (LLMs), but in multi-turn agentic tasks we find that the student model increases their reasoning lengths after training. Our empirical analysis shows that the reasoning token lengths is affected by how much the student can distract the teacher's scores. We introduce Muted Distillation (MD), a simple variant of OPD that hides the student's reasoning from the teacher, so the teacher judges what the student does without the interference of student's reasonings. MD takes a few lines of code and adds no extra data or hyperparameters. On the knowledge-work benchmarks OfficeQA Pro and SpreadsheetBench, it reduces output tokens per episode by 57\% and 53\% compared with standard OPD, making the student more concise than it was before training. At the same time, it matches OPD's accuracy on OfficeQA Pro and improves pass@1 by 4.8 points on SpreadsheetBench.

title: Feedback-Driven Prompt Refinement for Educational AI: Affective Trajectory Estimation and Bloom's Taxonomy Classification
summary: Contribution: This study has shown that a shared prompt-refinement procedure, guided by distinct affective and cognitive feedback signals, can improve held-out reference agreement and multi-label classification while reducing affective-generation variability without executor parameter updates. Background: Industry 4.0 has increased demand for personalized technical education across interconnected computing and engineering domains, while prompt sensitivity and generation variability have complicated dependable interpretation of instructional dialogue and learning outcomes. Research Questions: The study has examined whether task-specific feedback can improve affective-reference agreement, generation consistency, and cognitive classification without updating executor parameters. Methodology: A secondary language model has revised executor prompts using executor-output discrepancies against model-generated affective references for four dialogues and annotated Bloom labels for 70 learning outcomes; separate sets of 100 EduTalk conversations and 1,000 outcomes have supported held-out comparisons. Small refinement sets, unvalidated affective references, and absent learner-outcome measures have constrained interpretation. Findings: Affective mean absolute error has decreased from 0.742 to 0.702 and mean generation standard deviation from 0.307 to 0.238, while Bloom micro-F1 has increased from 0.687 to 0.893 and exact-match subset accuracy from 0.418 to 0.636. These findings have supported prompt refinement as a candidate approach for developing adaptive technical instruction, while its effects on workforce learning remain to be established.

title: A Hybrid Multi-Goal Path Planning Framework for Powered Wheelchairs in Dynamic Environments: From Simulation to Real-World Validation
comment: This work is under review at the International Journal of Social Robotics. The manuscript extends arXiv:2610.42049 by introducing an elliptical wheelchair model, enhanced local planning methods, and hardware validation
summary: Autonomous powered wheelchairs (PWs) operating in human-centered environments must combine efficient multi-destination path planning with continuous collision avoidance strategies in the presence of static and dynamic obstacles. This study presents a hybrid framework integrating Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP)-based global task ordering, Potential-Field (PF) guidance, and local Rapidly-exploring Random Tree (RRT) and A-star (A*) planners. PF guidance transfers global path information to local planners, helping the robot stay aligned with the global path during obstacle avoidance. Local planning is enhanced with direction-aware, extended-neighborhood A* or RRT using environment-aware sampling and two-step extension. The TSP-PF-RRT and TSP-PF-A* methods are evaluated in normal, crowded, and extra-crowded simulation environments using point-based and elliptical robot models. The elliptical model accounts for platform dimensions during collision avoidance phase. Hardware tests on the physical PW use motion capture (MoCap) for ground-truth measurements, while outside-MoCap experiments rely on onboard LiDAR and RGB-D sensing. Results show that incorporating the wheelchair geometry changes the observed collision behavior, yielding comparable collision avoidance performance between the two hybrid planners under the elliptical model.

title: Efficient Memory-Constrained Video Object Segmentation via Subspace Optimization
summary: Memory-based architectures for video object segmentation (VOS) have achieved remarkable performance by maintaining dense feature representations from past frames in a streaming Memory Bank. However, storing these features over time incurs substantial memory overhead and computational cost. In this work, we identify significant temporal redundancy in memory representations, where consecutive frames exhibit highly overlapping low-rank subspaces that remain stable over time. Building on this observation, we propose Memory Subspace Iteration (MSI), a training-free, model-agnostic plugin that exploits temporal subspace stability to efficiently compress streaming memory features. Extensive experiments on standard VOS benchmarks demonstrate that MSI preserves segmentation accuracy across multiple architectures while reducing the memory bank footprint by up to 25%. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/Hai-Anh-LE/MSI_WACV2027.

title: Advanced Reactance Method - A Novel Approach for Distance Protection in Presence of Grid-Following Inverter-Based-Resources
summary:
Renewable Energy Sources and consequently inverter-based resources (IBRs) are increasing worldwide.
  Grid-following (GFL) IBR control is the state-of-the-art.
  GFL IBRs exhibit different fault behavior compared to classical synchronous generators -- particularly in terms of Fault-Ride-Through (FRT) characteristics, which are critical for grid protection relaying.
  Grid protection must work securely, selectively and dependably, regardless of the feeding source.
  As common protection algorithms are designed for fault behavior determined by synchronous generators, their performance is expected to be compromised in the presence of GFL IBRs.
  Distance Protection is a widely used protection algorithm at all voltage levels.
  Literature shows that the FRT behavior of GFL IBRs impacts the Distance Protection relaying adversely.
  This paper proposes the Advanced Reactance Method, a further development of the Classical Reactance Method for Distance Protection in the presence of GFL IBRs.
  The key idea of the proposed method is to make the algorithm independent of the feeding source impedance.
  Therefore, the negative sequence voltage is taken into account along with the negative sequence current.
  This makes the algorithm independent of the FRT behavior of GFL IBRs, even in case of suppression of negative sequence current during unsymmetrical faults.
  Moreover, correct settings for the classical method in the presence of GFL IBRs are presented as a solution for relays without the advanced method.
  The novel algorithm is evaluated against the correctly parameterized Classical Reactance Method and the Distance Protection algorithm.

title: Neural Grey: Practical Vignetting Calibration from Casual Camera Rolls
summary: Neural Grey estimates a reusable camera-lens shading map from four approximate roll captures of a static, light-colored surface. Rolling the camera moves wall illumination across the sensor while lens shading stays fixed. We fit these two fields jointly, together with small pose and exposure errors, using a physical shading envelope and compact bounded neural residuals. Rotation alone, however, cannot distinguish radial lens attenuation from radial wall illumination. A focal-conditioned radial selector addresses this ambiguity: it uses focal length and sensor size to choose the broad radial profile while retaining the fitted spatial remainder. Component and sensitivity studies separate the roles of the field representation, radial selection, and numerical settings. Neural Grey reaches 25.43 dB on 100 synthetic cases, 24.49 dB on ray-traced lens architectures, and 25.38 dB on 21 real takes from seven optical configurations. On the real benchmark, it exceeds the strongest competing mean by 5.62 dB and wins five of seven configurations.

title: Digital Knockoffs
summary: Social simulations often use language model agents to represent people who differ on several measurable traits. However, describing a trait profile in a prompt does not guarantee the agent will express each trait at its intended level. We propose a method that calibrates agents to multidimensional profiles using activation steering: (i) extract steering directions for each trait, (ii) learn a shared mapping from steering strengths to measured trait scores, and (iii) search for a steering intervention for each target. We use Bayesian optimization for this search and evaluate the method on the Big Five personality scores of 500 OpenPsychometrics respondents. In each of five rounds, the assigned interventions yield lower mean absolute error across respondents than the prompting and steering baselines. Further, the model's responses to a given intervention yield the same trait profile regardless of whose target motivated it, so a poor match for one respondent can be the best match for another. When we match each respondent to the closest profile found across all tested interventions, Bayesian optimization yields 16.6% lower mean absolute error than uniform random search at the same evaluation budget. Our method thus offers a way to build social agents whose measured traits dovetail with those of the people they seek to represent. Whether this closer fit translates to improved predictions of downstream behavior remains an open question.

title: GERF: A Token-Efficient Multimodal Retrieval Framework for Schema-Guided Scientific Information Extraction
summary: Scientific information extraction (IE) is a fundamental component of AI for Science, transforming experimental knowledge embedded in scientific literature into structured and traceable data for evidence synthesis, scientific database construction, and data-driven discovery. However, critical experimental details are often distributed across text, tables, figures, captions, and surrounding discussion, making them difficult to recover using conventional text-only extraction. Existing LLM-based and multimodal RAG pipelines typically rely on full-document context or coarse page-level retrieval, introducing substantial irrelevant evidence and high textual and visual token costs. We propose GERF, a Graph-based Evidence Retrieval Framework for token-efficient, schema-guided multimodal scientific IE. GERF represents each article as a heterogeneous evidence graph that connects schema fields, text chunks, figures, and figure-derived content through semantic and structural relations. Using schema fields as retrieval anchors, GERF combines direct semantic retrieval, Random Walk with Restart, and null-aware evidence expansion to construct compact, field-specific multimodal evidence packages. Visual interpretation is applied only to graph-selected figures, avoiding indiscriminate processing of the entire document. We evaluate GERF from two complementary perspectives: evidence retrieval quality and pipeline-level input-token consumption. On the expert-annotated SOFC-Exp corpus, GERF retrieves gold-supported evidence for 94.55% of the evaluated field instances, providing broad field-level evidence coverage for downstream extraction. In the token comparison, GERF reduces average input-token usage by 73.40% relative to full-context processing and uses fewer tokens than the evaluated page-level pipelines.

title: Occupancy Planar Patch: Incremental Probabilistic Bounded-Plane Reconstruction from LiDAR Data
summary: Online surface reconstruction from LiDAR scans requires observation models that respect the sensor's physical measurement geometry. Unlike unordered point sets, LiDAR returns carry anisotropic range noise along known rays, which also implicitly identify free space. We introduce the Occupancy Planar Patch (OPP), an incremental bounded planar patch representation that evaluates surface likelihoods and free space directly in range-space, allowing sensor noise, plane uncertainty, and ray clearance to be explicitly modelled during reconstruction. A single ray-to-patch association weight jointly updates plane geometry, refines surface boundaries, and blends camera imagery. The method is evaluated using six sequences from the Oxford Spires and Multi-Campus datasets. OPP achieves the highest precision and lowest reconstruction error among evaluated methods, while producing stored maps among the most compact. By conservatively admitting surfaces only where geometric evidence is certain, OPP prioritises structural precision over unconstrained completeness, which is well suited for architectural modelling. Geometric reconstruction operates in real time, requiring 81 ms per frame on a representative sequence, with texture projection adding 134 ms.

title: Shallow may be better: Physics-Constrained Lightweight Networks for High-Throughput Particle Image Velocimetry
summary: Convolutional networks for optical flow typically adopt progressively deeper pyramidal encoders under the assumption that larger receptive fields improve motion estimation. For particle image velocimetry (PIV), however, tracer-particle displacement between frames is bounded by the acquisition geometry, allowing network depth to be derived from the physically admissible displacement rather than inherited from general-purpose architectures. Using a layer-by-layer analysis of spatial-support growth, we derive its explicit upper bound and show that deeper architectures substantially exceed the support required for PIV, compromising training stability, spatial resolution under particle loss, and inference efficiency. Based on this analysis, we develop LIMA3, a lightweight pyramidal displacement estimator with 589,000 trainable parameters. Across synthetic and experimental benchmarks, LIMA3 matches the accuracy of established learned and classical methods with at least an order of magnitude less memory and substantially higher throughput, while retaining the physically expected coarsening of spatial resolution as tracer information is lost. Its linear memory scaling enables megapixel processing within embedded memory budgets, such that LIMA3 can reach over 900 image pairs per second at $640\times480$~pixel on an RTX 5090 and 99 image pairs per second on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin. The spatial-support analysis provides a transferable design principle for compact optical-flow architectures and bounded-window attention, offering an alternative to compressing oversized general-purpose networks and enabling efficient operation alongside image acquisition.

title: Separating physics from discrepancy: Orthogonalized kernels for physics-encoded system identification
summary: Physics-encoded identification combines a physical model with a data-driven correction, but the data alone do not determine how the input-output map is split between them: components representable by the physical model may be assigned to either part. In kernel-based model embedding, this allocation is governed by the kernel. As a consequence, the physical parameters lack a well-defined target. In this work, this ambiguity is resolved a priori by defining a canonical physical parameter as the parameter of the physical model that best approximates the noise-free map, in a weighted least-squares sense, over a user-defined operating domain, together with an orthogonal discrepancy. Specifically, an orthogonalized kernel is derived that restricts the correction to functions orthogonal to the physical model. The resulting estimator keeps the closed-form solution of model embedding, while the canonical parameter depends only on the prescribed geometry, not on the kernel or the data. As the inputs become dense and the noise vanishes, the set of parameters consistent with the data converges to the canonical parameter, a property that generally fails without orthogonalization. Under energy-bounded noise, suitable regularization attains optimal worst-case estimation accuracy. Numerical examples demonstrate consistent parameter estimates across different kernels and experiments.

title: 3D-EMCAD: Efficient Multi-scale Convolutional Attention Decoding for Volumetric Brain Tumor Segmentation
comment: 7 pages, 4 figures, 1 table. Submitted to ICCIT 2026
summary: Encoder-decoder networks are widely used for volumetric brain tumor segmentation, yet recent trends favor high-capacity decoders that incur steep computational costs in 3D at high spatial resolutions. The Efficient Multi-scale Convolutional Attention Decoder (EMCAD) is a lightweight decoder that achieves strong accuracy at very low cost, but it has been validated only in 2D. Here, we extend EMCAD to volumetric segmentation (3D-EMCAD) by converting all operations to 3D and replacing standard normalization layers with group normalization to suit the small batch sizes of volumetric training. To isolate the impact of decoder choice, we evaluate five decoders: the proposed 3D-EMCAD, a vanilla SegResNet decoder, an Attention U-Net decoder, UNet++, and a plain U-Net decoder using an identical 3D SegResNet encoder and training protocol on BraTS 2020 (369 cases, three-fold cross-validation). The five decoders yield statistically indistinguishable performance: their mean Dice scores span only 0.0071, less than the fold-to-fold variation of most models, and a paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test shows no significant difference between 3D-EMCAD and three of the four baselines. Importantly, 3D-EMCAD achieves this shared accuracy with the fewest decoder parameters (1.15 M) and operations (8.6 G), requiring $7.3\times$ fewer operations than UNet++, which scores no higher. These findings demonstrate that decoder capacity beyond a modest budget offers no measurable benefit for volumetric brain tumor segmentation.

title: Digital Twins for Multi-Agent Systems: When to Trust, What to Change
summary: Digital twins of agent networks need to flag unreliable forecasts and help users choose interventions. Both decisions depend on what happens over several steps: an error can spread through the network, and an edit whose trajectory is easy to predict may still yield a poor collective outcome. We ask when information about error propagation improves failure detection and whether a learned twin can select effective network edits despite imperfect forecasts. We propose Propagation-Aware Validation for Networked Digital Twins (PAV-Twin). Its monitor combines Jacobian-based propagation features with recent errors and ensemble disagreement to estimate the risk that a forecast exceeds an error threshold. Its planner simulates each candidate edit and ranks the edits by their predicted collective outcomes. In simulations, the monitor gained 0.13 in area under the precision-recall curve on larger oscillator networks with familiar topologies and 0.09 on larger networks with held-out topologies, relative to a graph baseline without propagation features. Gains were small in contractive consensus. Giving the graph baseline the same features narrowed the gap. In a separate planning study, ensemble simulation recovered about 99% of the possible improvement over random intervention selection in oscillators and nearly all of it in consensus. With a simplified oscillator twin, selecting by predicted outcome also gave lower regret than selecting by trajectory fidelity. These results show when propagation features help flag unreliable forecasts and why the quality of intervention choices should be measured directly.

title: INSEP: Refusal-Direction Inseparability as a Defense Against Abliteration
summary: Abliteration is a widely used white-box attack against the safety alignment of large language models (LLMs). It elicits harmful behavior by estimating a refusal direction in the model's activation space and projecting that direction out of the residual-stream write-out matrices. We propose INSEP, a defense that fine-tunes the model to reduce the separability of harmful and benign activations along the refusal direction. Abliteration estimates this direction as a difference in class means and projects it out. Reducing separability weakens the signal the attack relies on. An adversarial eigendecomposition selects the most separable prompt subsets. A low-rank adapter reduces their separation along that direction. Behavioral losses preserve the base model's refusal and the quality of its benign responses during training. We benchmark INSEP against six published defenses under five attacks, across eight LLMs from 1B to 14B parameters and several model families. Beyond response harm, we measure coherence, directness, over-refusal, and MMLU, to distinguish robust refusal from low harm produced by evasive or degraded responses. INSEP ranks first on the mean composite score across all eight base models while retaining utility, in the largest abliteration-defense evaluation reported to date.

title: ScaleEvals: Scaling Generalist Policy Evaluation through Reset-Free Autonomous Play
summary: Real-world evaluation of generalist robot policies is bottlenecked by manual resets, human grading, and small fixed task suites with limited diagnostic coverage. We present ScaleEvals, a scalable reset-free protocol that evaluates policies through continuous physical play across a robot fleet. A VLM AutoPrompter generates scene-grounded tasks with difficulty estimates, language prompts, and skill tags, enabling performance analysis across diverse rollouts. A VLM AutoGrader assesses task progress, achieving 90.7% agreement with human graders. Scores are aggregated via a soft-win Bradley-Terry model, while tag-stratified ANOVA provides interpretable capability diagnostics. Across 3,000+ physical autonomous rollouts on DROID and YAM, ScaleEvals achieves 23.0 net rollouts/hr per station while reducing active human labor by 98%. By ranking five SOTA generalist policies, ScaleEvals correlates with held-out manual evaluation ranking on DROID (r=0.94, rho=0.90, p=0.018), and remains internally consistent on a second embodiment, YAM (r=0.839, rho=0.80). Beyond aggregate rankings, we observe behavioral compositionality: recombining verb-, skill-, and object-conditioned evidence predicts policy order on unseen prompts. Across 10 tasks and 240 prospective physical rollouts, we recover three-policy orderings of 96% pairwise concordance, demonstrating ScaleEvals can predict not just which policy leads, but where rankings reverse.

title: Every IVUS Frame in Its Place: A Zero-Install Browser Tool for Registering Intravascular Ultrasound to the Coronary Angiogram, and a Path to Angiography-Only Plaque Imaging
comment: 19 pages, 10 figures, 4 tables. Live tool with one-click demo: https://menonpg.github.io/ivus-xa-registration/?demo
summary: Intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) shows plaque composition, calcium and stent apposition that the coronary angiogram cannot, but relating each IVUS cross-section to its position on the angiogram is still largely done in the operator's head. Commercial co-registration is tied to vendor consoles and to set-up at acquisition, so archived angiograms and pullbacks cannot be co-registered, and paired data for training AI models remain scarce. We present a semi-automatic registration tool that runs entirely in a web browser, with no installation and no upload. The clinician picks a contrast-filled reference frame (aided by automatic contrast and cardiac-phase analysis), selects or traces the vessel centerline (aided by Frangi vesselness and minimal paths), and pins the pullback ends and visible landmarks; a monotone piecewise-linear map then places every IVUS frame on the vessel, and each case exports as a frame-level training record. The original Python analysis runs unchanged in WebAssembly and videos are decoded frame-accurately with WebCodecs. On 6 angiographic runs the in-browser analysis was bit-identical to the server pipeline on identical frames; browser decoding differed by at most 2 grey levels, suggested reference frames agreed in all runs and the default automatic centerline in 4 of 6. A 546-frame pullback decoded in 5.3 s. On 36 phantoms with known ground truth, the clinician-guided trace stayed inside the lumen along 87-99% of the vessel, whereas the fully automatic centerline fell from 83% to 0% as noise rose and contrast fell. In a registered Left Main case, one side-branch landmark moved mid-pullback positions by 17.5% of the segment. We map where AI can enter each step, up to predicting a virtual IVUS from the angiogram alone, and make the tool freely available online with a one-click demo.

title: Suppressing Chaos Without Silencing Excitable Oscillators
comment: 14 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to International Journal of Bifurcation and Chaos
summary: A negative Lyapunov exponent is not a sufficient goal for controlling an excitable oscillator. A gain can remove chaos by removing the excitation that the model is meant to keep. This manuscript studies that failure mode in three models: the forced FitzHugh--Nagumo neuron, the forced Aliev--Panfilov cardiac cell, and the autonomous Hindmarsh--Rose neuron. Chaos is measured by the largest state Lyapunov exponent. Excitation is measured by threshold crossings, by the excursion of the fast variable, and by the firing rate. Recovery damping, tracking of an unstable periodic orbit, Pyragas delayed feedback, and a change of the fast time scale are compared on the same chaotic regimes. In the forced models, large damping and large rate changes reach regularity by silencing the cell, while tracking and delayed feedback keep firing. In the autonomous model, recovery damping raises the firing rate several-fold instead. A classical matrix-measure bound links these outcomes to the channel through which the gain acts. A constant-metric contraction certificate coexists with substantial firing only under tracking, which subtracts a gain from the fast direction.

title: Where does pancreatic lesion segmentation fail on public CT? An attenuation-stratified analysis of a duct-guided pipeline on PanTS
summary: Lesion segmentation is a building block of most CT pipelines for pancreatic cancer detection, yet lesion overlap scores stay low. Instead of proposing a new architecture, we report where an end-to-end pipeline fails on a large public dataset. On PanTS we built a three-stage pipeline: pancreas segmentation, maps of the main pancreatic duct (MPD) and common bile duct (CBD), and a lesion model that receives the CT with or without the predicted duct maps. Both lesion models were trained identically on 4007 scans and evaluated once on 737 held-out test scans (127 with a lesion) under a comparison rule fixed before the test run. Lesion Dice was 0.213 with duct maps and 0.209 with CT only (paired difference +0.004, 95% CI -0.011 to +0.019). The duct maps raised the share of lesions touched by a prediction (+0.079, 95% CI +0.024 to +0.134) but also enlarged predictions in lesion-free scans, and lesion-like regions were predicted in all lesion-free test scans. Out of fold, keeping only the predicted components that touched the lesion raised Dice only from 0.285 to 0.309; the loss came mainly from the extent of correctly located predictions. Clearly hypoattenuating lesions, which intensity alone separates from normal pancreas, had the lowest coverage (median 16.6%). From the predicted maps alone, the MPD diameter separated lesion from lesion-free test scans with AUC 0.794 (95% CI 0.747 to 0.839), while the CBD diameter was weak (AUC 0.603) and added nothing. Code for training, inference and evaluation is publicly available.

title: SupportChain: Trace-Calibrated Aggregation of Quote-Grounded Reasoning Chains for Multi-Hop RAG with Small Readers
summary: Strong results in multi-hop retrieval-augmented question answering come from graph indexes read by models of 70B parameters or more, and building such an index calls a large language model over the whole corpus. We present SupportChain, which splits a question into hops, binds each hop's answer to a sentence quoted from a retrieved passage, estimates how reliable each execution is from its own trace, and merges several executions by the support of their answers, the pooled reliability of the executions that agree, stopping once support is high enough. With a 9B reader under the HippoRAG~2 protocol, SupportChain reaches 63.0 F1 on MuSiQue, above the best earlier result of 59.2, which used a 20B reader. With the same reader and embedder, it is significantly better than HippoRAG~2 on all five datasets, by up to 17.2 F1, and it builds no index. Merging by support is significantly better than majority voting, and than letting the reader choose among the candidates, on three of the five datasets and level with both on the other two. The reliability model needs only 100 answered training questions.

title: Selection Policies for Equal-Byte Mixed-Precision Quantization of Small Language Models
summary: Can changing which matrices receive 2, 4, or 8 bits improve a small language model without increasing its parameter storage? I compare two parent-selection rules in the same genetic algorithm: a binary-tournament variant and an Alternis-inspired rule. A separate baseline samples repaired random allocations without crossover or mutation. All three use the same MLX affine quantizer, byte ceiling, initialization and candidate allowance within each study. An exploratory study on Qwen3.5-2B evaluates 90 allocations per run. The main study on Qwen3-1.7B evaluates 500 distinct allocations per run over 10 paired seeds. Against uniform four-bit, tournament reduces held-out next-token negative log-likelihood (NLL) by 0.0616 on AG News and 0.0152 on IMDb on average, improving all 10 seeds on each corpus at identical parameter storage. Alternis improves five seeds and ties five on AG News; on IMDb its mean gain is near zero. Random returns uniform four-bit in every seed. The tournament representative answers 156 of 400 ARC-Challenge questions correctly versus 163 for uniform; no accuracy gain is demonstrated on this subset. The result favors this tournament variant for text prediction under the tested protocol, not for compression ratio or task accuracy.

title: Belief-Driven Quantum Magnetometer Control for GPS-Denied Navigation
summary: Autonomous vehicles increasingly need to navigate without satellite positioning. Magnetic anomaly navigation (Mag-Nav) with quantum magnetometers offers a passive, unjammable fix, but the low size-weight-and-power (SWaP) sensors that small drones can carry are weak, and they are operated open loop at a fixed setting. Interferometric (Ramsey) magnetometers face a trade-off: long interrogation times are more sensitive but become ambiguous when the expected field is uncertain. The navigator's own position belief, pushed through the anomaly map, predicts that field. We close this loop. The filter's predictive field distribution sets the Ramsey phase and interrogation time at every epoch, through a closed-form rule that moves between an ambiguity limit and a decoherence limit. We evaluate it on real U.S. Air Force flight data (real tracks, inertial drift, measured fields, and a survey map tested 18 months after it was flown), with only the Ramsey sensor modelled. Against fixed-setting baselines, 63 of 72 independent flight windows favour belief driven sensing ($p = 2 \times 10^{-11}$). Error falls by 20-27% for low-SNR sensors and 30-44% for mid-contrast sensors. An ablation separates the two ingredients. Phase alignment drives the gain in steady flight, and the rule matches the best fixed setting without the hindsight tuning that setting requires. After a lost start, interrogation time adaptation is essential, cutting median error by 37-42% even against hindsight-tuned phase-aligned settings. Gains are small for high-quality sensors with accurate maps. On an IBM superconducting qubit, the rule's interrogation time stays within $1.3\times$ of the empirical optimum. Coupled with information-aware routing, belief-driven sensing lowers mission error by 15-40%.

title: Teacher-Guided Multimodal Dual Representation Reconstruction for Egocentric Human Activity Recognition
summary: Multimodal Egocentric Human Activity Recognition (Ego-HAR) leverages complementary cues from first-person vision (V) and inertial sensor data (S) to recognize daily activities, where video mainly captures appearance and object-related context while inertial signals capture motion cues that video may miss. However, existing pre-training methods typically supervise the fused representation with a single joint objective, which may underemphasize the complementarity between the two modalities and limit the model's ability to learn from distinct modality-oriented signals. To address this issue, we propose Multimodal Dual Representation Reconstruction (MDR2), a teacher-guided pre-training framework in which frozen, label-informed video and inertial teachers each provide dense, modality-specific targets to a multimodal student trained on temporally sparse inputs. On the EvIs-Kitchen dataset, MDR2 improves noun/verb F1-macro over the supervised M-Baseline by 9.20/6.17 points at K=4 video key frames and by 1.21/1.82 points at K=32. These results show that MDR2 consistently achieves higher mean recognition performance across the evaluated video-observation settings under the unified backbone setting, with more pronounced gains under sparse inputs.

title: Deliverable Frequency Regulation Reserve for VPPs via Transmission-Distribution Co-Simulation
comment: Submitted to the 2027 IEEE Power & Energy Society General Meeting (PESGM)
summary: Aggregations of distributed energy resources can provide frequency regulation services. However, device-level power headroom may not accurately represent the power deliverable at the transmission-distribution interface. This paper proposes a bidirectional, storage-aware power-sharing framework for a virtual power plant (VPP). Delivery factors obtained from the perturbations used to construct the voltage-sensitivity matrix account for feeder losses and voltage-dependent loads, while battery energy limits and state-of-charge weights are included in the allocation. The framework is evaluated using the IEEE 8500-node feeder and IEEE 14-bus system. The proposed method tracks the feeder-head request within 2% compared with 23-26% over-delivery under the injection-headroom framework. It also sustains the requested power response 22% longer before reaching the storage energy limit. Moreover, communicating the updated VPP reserve to the transmission system operator reduces the post-transient integrated area control error by 80% relative to fixed reserve registration.

title: Generalizable Variable-Rate Adaptation for Image Coding for Machines
comment: Accepted to 2026 IEEE International Conference on Visual Communications and Image Processing (IEEE VCIP 2026)
summary: Image Coding for Machines (ICM) aims to preserve task-relevant information for machine vision under limited bitrates. However, most ICM models are trained for a fixed operating point, and extending them to variable-rate compression is challenging because their training objectives differ across tasks and model designs. In this paper, we propose a loss-agnostic distillation framework for variable-rate ICM. A pretrained fixed-rate ICM model is used as a frozen teacher, while a student model learns variable-rate behavior through importance-adaptive quantization and distillation-based optimization. This enables continuous bitrate control with a single model while preserving task-relevant latent components, without requiring the original task-specific loss or downstream task labels. Experiments based on existing ICM models demonstrate that the proposed method provides continuous bitrate control and achieves competitive recognition performance compared with the fixed-rate models.

title: Information Access and Gain-Loss Framing in Six Large Language Models and Human Decision Makers
comment: 19 pages, 3 figures. Code and model outputs: https://github.com/aadycm/Humans-Vs-LLM-Research
summary: A risky choice can be described by what will be saved or what will be lost, and people often choose differently depending on that wording. We test whether six large language models (LLMs) show this gain-loss framing effect, and whether it shrinks when they can first read more about the options. GPT-4.1, GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Qwen3 235B and Llama 4 Maverick made 11,519 choices across four risk scenarios, each in its original wording, two paraphrases and a mirrored version in the opposite wording. Before choosing, a model could open up to 0, 2, 3 or 4 of seven information cards. With no cards, all six models showed large framing effects: the share choosing the safe option was 27 to 79 percentage points lower under loss than under gain wording. The gap was smaller at 2 cards than with no cards in every model. Against a 10-point threshold set in our analysis plan, GPT-4.1 fell within it at 4 cards and Qwen3 only at 2 cards; in the plan's pooled comparison over all versions, GPT-4.1 was within it from 2 cards and GPT-4o from 3. GPT-4o-mini and Llama 4 Maverick kept gaps of 28 to 66 points with cards, and for GPT-4o-mini and Qwen3 the gap grew again from 2 to 4 cards. Part of the drop from 0 to 2 cards may reflect a change in prompt format, and most card content counted against the risky option, which may favor the safe choice. In an exploratory comparison with 198 students who saw the same scenarios and cards but opened cards one at a time and chose how many, decisions made after opening 0 or 1 cards showed a 19-point difference between the gain scenarios, asked first, and the loss scenarios, asked later, and no clear difference appeared in decisions made after opening more, though this design cannot show that cards reduced framing in people. With these cards, in the balanced comparison 17 of 18 card gaps were below the model's no-card gap, but few were within the threshold.

title: MatHarness: Towards Long-Horizon Open-ended AutoResearch for Computational Materials Science
summary: Materials science research is a non-linear, long-horizon process. Existing scientific agents, however, largely rely on specific task execution or predefined workflows, rendering them brittle in open-ended settings. To bridge this gap, we present MatHarness, an agent harness designed for open-ended, long-horizon computational materials research spanning the complete lifecycle from initial ideation to manuscript writing. MatHarness couples three mechanisms: execution robustness through pre-flight verification, expert-distilled skills, and just-in-time auditing; epistemic adaptability through persistent research artifacts and an evolving scientific mental model; and collective intelligence through a heterogeneous multi-agent round table under targeted human oversight. We evaluate MatHarness on adsorbate-induced surface segregation in Cu-Zn alloys, an open question in methanol-synthesis catalysis. Over a multi-week trajectory consuming roughly 10^3 GPU-hours (50 production DFT relaxations prescreened by 171 machine-learning-potential evaluations) the system revised its plan six times, recovered autonomously from failed calculations, and had an independent auditor overturn one of its own over-attributed claims before publication. Within the sampled metallic dilute-limit models, the validated DFT analysis supports an adsorbate-induced tendency toward greater surface Cu exposure at both composition endpoints, with facet- and coverage-dependent exceptions. These results were compiled into a complete manuscript with human involvement concentrated in specification, approval, and strategic steering gates. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/PrentisAI/pippin.

title: LoKiTO: Local Kinodynamic Trajectory Optimization for UAVs based on Memory-Efficient Neural Distance Fields
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures, submitted to IEEE RA-L (under review)
summary: This paper introduces LoKiTO, a 3D local kinodynamic trajectory optimizer that combines a Chebyshev polynomial parameterization with an online neural Euclidean Signed Distance Field (ESDF) representation for aerial robotics. While current gradient-based planners often struggle with the high memory requirements of explicit volumetric maps or fail to strictly enforce dynamic limits, LoKiTO embeds kinodynamic constraints directly into a modular cost function and exploits the numerical conditioning properties of the Chebyshev basis. Collision awareness is provided by a continuous, memory-efficient neural ESDF updated online from LiDAR measurements, which drastically reduces map memory consumption to approximately 1.0 MB. Benchmarking in highly cluttered simulated environments against state-of-the-art baselines (Fast-Planner and EGO-Planner) demonstrates the superiority of our approach. Experimental results show that LoKiTO achieves over 99.4% dynamic feasibility compliance, significantly outperforming the baselines, and maintaining higher median clearance from obstacles. By coupling a well-conditioned continuous parameterization with explicit kinodynamic reasoning, LoKiTO provides a practical and extensible basis for local replanning in aerial robotics.

title: When Recognition Meets Discovery: Learning Need Not Be Entangled in One Representation Space
summary: Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) aims to recognize known classes while discovering novel categories from unlabeled data containing both old and novel samples. Existing methods typically optimize recognition and discovery within a shared representation space, implicitly assuming that the same representation geometry can serve both objectives. Through controlled spectral analysis, we uncover a striking asymmetry: old-class discrimination is increasingly concentrated in the dominant singular directions, while novel-class structure is better preserved in the complementary residual space. More importantly, strengthening the former can even degrade the latter, revealing that recognition and discovery compete for representation capacity rather than merely for optimization weight. Motivated by this observation, we propose Dual-Space Spectral Routing, which dynamically decomposes the representation via online SVD and routes supervised recognition and unsupervised discovery to complementary discriminative and general subspaces. We further exploit their distinct responses to old and novel samples to construct a dual-space novelty signal, which guides Subspace Relation Aggregation (SRA) for organizing candidate novel categories. Extensive experiments across multiple GCD baselines, backbones, and benchmarks demonstrate a consistently improved recognition-discovery balance without introducing additional inference parameters. Code will be open source.

title: Neural Costate Guidance for Autonomous Cislunar Low-Thrust Trajectory Generation
summary: Future missions will benefit from onboard autonomous low-thrust trajectory generation to correct deviations from the nominal flight path caused by navigation errors and thruster outages. Onboard computing resources rarely allow the solution of a cold-started, long-duration nonconvex optimal control problem, especially in dynamically challenging regions such as the cislunar to translunar corridor of the Earth-Moon system. This paper develops data augmentation and training techniques that enable a neural network to predict accurate initial costates of the indirect method. A recovery trajectory is then built from repeated network queries in a computationally efficient guidance algorithm. Training data are produced by the backward generation of optimal examples method, extending prior approaches to the circular restricted three-body problem. A novel anchor trajectory approach is developed to cover the relevant state space, and costate rescaling and a Hamiltonian loss term are used to improve learning. The method is demonstrated on Earth-Moon transfers from a high Earth orbit to halo orbits about L1 and L2. Under navigation errors and thruster outages, a spacecraft reaches the target orbit more often with the proposed method than with nominal-trajectory tracking or fully numerical reoptimization. Onboard computation is reduced by more than an order of magnitude compared with reoptimization.

title: Geospatial foundation models and deep learning for climate resilience: a review of transfer, uncertainty and decision readiness
comment: 16 pages, 8 figures, 6 tables. Preprint submitted to Frontiers in Climate
summary: Geospatial foundation models can reuse information learned from large Earth-observation archives, but their value for climate resilience depends on whether that information transfers to unfamiliar events, regions and observing conditions. This review connects advances in deep learning with the evidence needed for hazard monitoring and early warning. A descriptive audit of 137 full-text hazard-application studies is interpreted alongside a separate corpus of 37 model and benchmark records. Ninety-eight application studies reported an out-of-distribution experiment, whereas headline evaluations included held-out events in 31 studies, regions in 25 and sensors in only two. None of the ten studies coded for geospatial foundation-model fine-tuning used sensor holdout as a headline test. Uncertainty-related methods were recorded in 16 studies, including two with explicitly calibrated probabilistic output. These overlapping counts describe evaluation practice within the coded corpus, not a ranking of model families. We distinguish Earth-observation representation learning from atmospheric forecasting and examine how labels, observability, forecast lead time and decision requirements constrain their contribution across flood, wildfire, drought, heat, cryosphere and cascading-hazard applications. We then develop a decision-backward evaluation framework: define the action and information available when it must be taken, reproduce the relevant shift, retain a matched task-specific baseline, and report misses, false alarms, reliability and end-to-end latency. The framework turns transferability from a broad model claim into a testable requirement for climate adaptation and risk management.

title: BIRD-Persona: A Persona-Aware Benchmark for SQL and pandas Analytics Code Generation
summary: Production text-to-code systems use large language models to turn natural-language analytics requests into executable SQL and pandas code. Existing benchmarks cover both tasks but do not isolate when performance diverges between them. We introduce BIRD-Persona, a persona-stratified extension of BIRD-Python that adds novice and expert rewrites to tasks with matched SQL and pandas ground truth, along with schema variants and task-structure annotations. Across 1,534 tasks, nine models, and 245,592 evaluations, SQL outperforms pandas for eight of nine systems. The gap varies by condition: expert, schema-explicit prompts improve both paradigms but help SQL more; schema representations have mixed, model-dependent effects; and selected-column burden widens the gap while subqueries do not. By making user phrasing a controlled benchmark dimension, BIRD-Persona supports persona-aware and paradigm-aware evaluation of natural-language analytics systems. The dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/optum-cognition-lab/BIRD-Persona.

title: Decision models for UAVBench and the viability of edge deployment
summary: Small language models are often proposed for reasoning onboard a drone. However, a good benchmark score does not tell us whether a model will actually run, and run usefully, on an edge computer. In this paper we study three related questions using the UAV decision benchmark, UAVBench. First, are small structured decision models good candidates for these tasks? Second, can an ordinary local machine (a Mac) screen candidate models before we test them on physical devices? Third, what software and resource limits govern deployment? Our main Mac evaluation covers 24 model configurations on the same 2,000 validated multiple-choice questions from UAVBench. These include 20 size-and-precision configurations of 11 generative models, plus four open-weight structured decision models that received no additional UAVBench-specific training. A structured decision model, H2O Lightning 4B, achieved the highest accuracy we observed, scoring 77.65% on the Mac. This shows that these models are well suited to this kind of task. However, when we tried to deploy the decision models, we ran into conversion and runtime limits on the edge devices we tested, which we describe in detail. To test local screening, we ran matched evaluations of two generative models on both the Mac and a Qualcomm RB3 board. The accuracies did not match exactly, but the ranking did. LFM2 2.6B ranked above Qwen2.5 1.5B on both platforms. This supports using a local machine to shortlist candidates. That said, individual answers still differed between platforms, so testing on the actual hardware remained necessary.

title: AlpaSafe: Risk-Aware Trajectory Selection for Vision-Language-Action Models in Autonomous Driving
summary: Reasoning-based driving vision-language-action (VLA) models propose multiple candidate trajectories at each decision, yet only one is executed. Standard evaluation scores the best candidate, assuming an oracle selector that deployment lacks, and leaves the risk of the executed candidate unexamined. Existing online evaluators typically close this gap with a purpose-trained scene or world model, often rolling out each candidate through it at inference time. We introduce AlpaSafe, a risk-aware trajectory selector that reuses the scene representation a frozen driving VLA computes while proposing its candidates. AlpaSafe reads the last hidden token of the VLA's prompt prefill. A lightweight head, trained on the closed-loop simulation outcomes of the candidates, fuses this token with each candidate trajectory and predicts a relative score and collision/offroad logits. A fixed rule removes candidates dominated on the two risk logits and selects the highest-scoring candidate among those remaining, adding neither rollouts nor VLA training. Experiments on 525 AlpaSim scenes show that AlpaSafe outperforms Alpamayo's default first-sample rule and uniform random selection in selected regret and top-1 agreement, and reduces the collision-at-fault or offroad rate from 6.41% and 6.10% to 4.93%. The selector has 1.7M parameters and takes 0.75 ms per decision.

title: VTree: Question-Driven Growth of Hierarchical Memory for Agentic Long-Video Understanding
summary: Long videos spanning tens of minutes to hours far exceed the context window of today's vision-language models, and the standard remedy of sparse uniform frame sampling discards exactly the fine-grained evidence that specific questions depend on. Existing video agents explore on demand but re-explore from scratch for every question and discard their exploration state once an answer is produced, so per-question cost scales with video length. Hierarchical-memory methods instead fix the scope of each depth in advance and deepen along a pre-committed pyramid rather than toward the question. We observe that a video's coarse structure (where its scenes and topics begin and end) is question-independent, whereas which part a question must zoom into, and how deep, is question-dependent. We propose VTree, which builds a coarse hierarchical memory tree over a video once and then, for each question, grows branches only where that question needs depth. The growth is globally routed so any part of the timeline is reachable, sufficiency-gated so drilling stops when the evidence suffices, and query-conditioned so a branch unfolds into the sub-intervals that answer \emph{this} question. Crucially, every expansion is written back into the video memory, allowing later questions to reuse previously discovered structure and evidence without repeating the corresponding expansion process. Across five long-video understanding benchmarks, VTree consistently improves the accuracy of diverse vision-language backbones while substantially reducing the context length and execution time required for each question.

title: Effect of Transmission Line Switching on Damping of Interarea Modes
summary: This paper will explore the impact of switching transmission lines on the damping of interarea oscillation modes. This phenomenon played a central role in the 2025 Iberian blackout and in some North American oscillation events. The paper first assesses the effectiveness of line switching for enhancing mode damping by studying the problem in classical test power systems. The paper then tests these observations in realistic large-scale models of the Western Interconnection that represent recent real-time system conditions. It is shown that the switching of key transmission lines can have a significant impact on the damping of inter-area modes depending on system operating conditions.

title: Demographic Encoding is Not Exposure: Fairness and Privacy in Chest X-ray Foundation Models
summary: Medical foundation models encode patient demographics and can reveal whether a patient was in the training set, and these properties are often treated as one problem. We tested whether they are aligned by measuring demographic encoding, diagnostic fairness gaps and membership-inference vulnerability on the same models. We trained 200 linear or multilayer-perceptron (MLP) heads on frozen BiomedCLIP, DINOv2 and RAD-DINO embeddings, with three seeds, and audited them on CheXpert and NIH ChestX-ray14. Demographic encoding explained almost no variance in patient vulnerability, and all 72 CheXpert associations were statistically equivalent to zero. Erasing linearly decodable demographics left leakage unchanged but reduced age-related underdiagnosis gaps. Leakage depended instead on head capacity and training length. On RAD-DINO, a linear head reached a membership-inference area under the curve (AUC) of 0.694, compared with 0.907 for a 30-epoch MLP, at similar test performance. Fairness and privacy should therefore be audited separately, and linear heads or shorter training reduce leakage with little or no loss of utility. The code is available on GitHub for public use.

title: From Reward Engineering to Data-Centric Reinforcement Learning for Effective Agentic Visual Tool Use
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) increasingly use external visual tools to acquire evidence during reasoning, yet learning when to invoke these tools remains challenging. Existing tool-use reinforcement learning (RL) methods often rely on call-contingent rewards to encourage beneficial tool use, but such reward engineering can distort the task objective and lead to degenerate calling behaviors. We argue that effective tool-use learning requires identifying not merely which questions are difficult, but which failures are attributable to missing visual evidence and can therefore be corrected through tool observations. We propose AOVO, a data-centric framework that enables MLLMs to learn effective tool use through perception attribution and policy-adaptive data sampling (PADS), without introducing tool-specific rewards. It counterfactually probes the model's reasoning states to identify observation-sensitive questions, distinguishing them from reasoning-dominated ones. PADS then periodically estimates category-level observation effects from recent policy rollouts and dynamically reallocates the training distribution toward questions where visual observations provide informative learning signals, while optimizing solely for final-answer correctness. Experiments across diverse visual perception and multimodal reasoning benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over competitive tool-use MLLMs, with causal analysis further validating the data-centric perspective for learning effective visual tool use.

title: When Tools Fail, Agents Fabricate: Silent Failure and Verification-First Oversight in Tool-Using LLM Agents
comment: NeurIPS 2026 Workshop: Who Verifies the Agents? Toward Reliable Agent Development. 12 pages, 3 figures, 7 tables
summary: Tool-using LLM agents must recover when a tool call fails, by retrying, switching tools, or revising their plan. We study how agents fail when tools fail, using RetryRealistic, a sandboxed yet realistic testbed for controlled fault injection in which agents operate on a real OS filesystem with genuine permission enforcement, SQLite databases, a deterministic local HTTP server, and a constrained shell, across 8 tools, 9 fault types with controlled persistence, and 30 multi-step tasks. Evaluating four agents over 2,100 faulted runs against ground truth, we find that recovery is unreliable (19-68% correct) and frequently silent: 6-26% of runs end in a confident fabrication, a wrong answer asserted as fact. The failure mode is governed more by the fault type than by the model: faults that return partial data drive fabrication (up to 38%), while hard denials drive honest failure. The mechanism is what we call silent ingestion: the agent accepts faulted data as valid on first contact without retrying or flagging the problem, then builds a fabricated answer on top of it. We show that fabrication is reducible: a verification-first Monitor, grounding checks in structured tool outputs and issuing corrective directives rather than hard blocks, raises correct recovery from 45.6% to 56.3% and cuts fabrication from 17.3% to 10.8%. Removing chain-of-thought increases fabrication (+8.3pp), so deliberation guards against silent ingestion. We release RetryRealistic, the fault-injection toolkit, and all annotated traces at https://github.com/Kingsford-Group/RetryRealistic

title: Lifted Multiple Shooting for Parallel-in-Time Contact-Rich Trajectory Optimization
summary: Planning through contact requires accounting for the coupled dynamics of a robot and its environment, including inertial effects, contact forces, and friction. However, the non-smoothness and multimodality of contact dynamics and contact geometry makes gradient-based optimization challenging. In this work, we propose lifted multiple shooting, a trajectory optimization transcription that can be solved directly using nonlinear program solvers. By introducing contact impulses as optimization variables, our formulation allows the optimizer to satisfy the state-transition constraints using friction-cone-feasible impulses while separately enforcing their consistency with the contact model. Our formulation supports a broad class of contact constitutive relations, with sensitivities computed through implicit differentiation. To enable efficient planning over long horizons and for high-dimensional systems, we further introduce IP-PAS, a parallel-in-time primal-dual interior-point solver that achieves O(log T) parallel computational depth. We evaluate the proposed methods on six fully dynamic contact-rich planning tasks, including nonprehensile pushing and in-hand manipulation, without contact-guiding costs. Lifted multiple shooting improves success rates by up to 81.5 percentage points over standard multiple shooting, while IP-PAS achieves solution quality comparable to serial methods with up to a 3.1x speedup and scales to horizons of 40,000 timesteps.

title: LightOnOCR for AMNLT: Reading Chant Notation and Lyrics in One Pass, from Single Staves to Whole Pages
summary: Aligned music notation and lyrics transcription (AMNLT) asks for the notes of a chant, its sung text and the assignment of syllables to notes in one output. Fuentes-Martínez et al., who defined the task, found that the one vision-language model they tested fell far behind specialised recognisers. We fine-tune LightOnOCR-3-1B, a page OCR model with one billion parameters, end to end, vision encoder included, to write a staff as a GABC string whose letters denote staff positions. Trained on the published AMNLT training split alone, it more than halves the best published aligned music and lyrics error rate (AMLER) on Solesmes, the one directly comparable dataset (9.9 against 21.0 %); on Einsiedeln and Salzinnes, measured in a different encoding, its figures are also lower. The benchmark does not measure generalisation to unseen manuscripts: while the pitch error on AMNLT validation stays between 1.7 and 1.9 %, on 200 staves from five unseen manuscripts it falls from 24.9 to 1.3 % as we add chant aligned through CantusDB, Transkribus ground truth and silver staves kept only where two readers agree. Trained also on multi-staff images, it reads whole pages without staff detection (pitch error 3.3 to 3.8 % on validation and test pages, 1.9 % on pages of unseen manuscripts). Remaining errors include Gothic F clefs read as C clefs, notes dropped with abbreviated or illegible text and lower accuracy on pages with small notation. Controlled ablations are needed to explain the gains.

title: Scaled Relative Graph Separation for Unbounded Nonlinear Systems
comment: An extended version of a conference paper accepted for the 65th IEEE Conference on Decision and Control, 2026
summary: We investigate stability analysis of one-channel nonlinear feedback systems based on the recent notion of scaled relative graph (SRG). Our focus is on the SRG separation in the complex plane for feedback stability analysis that involves possibly unbounded open-loop nonlinear systems. Subject to a technical assumption, a homotopy-based SRG separation theorem is developed as the main result, where the incremental directed gap is utilized as a key instrument to quantify robust feedback stability along the homotopy path. Doing so enables us to incorporate commonly used integrators as unbounded systems in the SRG-based framework. Specializations of the main result to linear systems, along with illustrative examples, are also provided to demonstrate its effectiveness.

title: Separating Module Gain From Transport Plan Contribution in Audio-Visual Dynamic Facial Expression Recognition
summary: A cross-modal routing module can improve over its backbone while its transport plan accounts for no demonstrable part of that improvement. In ABVnet with DFEW, Sinkhorn cross-modal routing (SCR) exceeds the retrained baseline by 0.87 unweighted average recall (UAR) points, a resolved difference, yet sits 0.17 points above an individually trained, parameter-matched pooled variant, an unresolved difference that establishes no equivalence; under the development protocol the comparison with the baseline reverses. Separating the two needs comparisons a module-against-backbone test cannot supply: parameter-matched variants changing only the plan rule, and interventions replacing the plan without retraining. The evaluation covers MMA-DFER and ABVnet on DFEW and MAFW, and MMA-DFER on CREMA-D, with a single training run per configuration and paired fold intervals. ABVnet with DFEW motivated the follow-up after the broader results were available. Replacing the plan everywhere with a uniform one reduces UAR by 0.72, whereas permuting its rows gives an unresolved difference of -0.20 UAR points; permutation is less damaging by 0.51 UAR points, a resolved contrast. Replacing the plan with the product of its own marginals, preserving both marginals and removing only frame-specific mixtures, reduces UAR by 0.70. These reductions concern reliance at inference; attribution of the module gain to the transport plan remains unestablished. Under the 1.5 fold-dependence widening, the baseline gain remains resolved, whereas the replacement reductions and the paired contrast are unresolved.

title: Tool-to-Self: Internalizing Visual Tool Capabilities via Scaffolded Reinforcement Learning
